title: Menu complexity of approximately revenue-optimal multi-item auctions
short_statement: When selling $n$ items to one additive buyer with independent values, how many menu (lottery) options are needed to guarantee a $(1-\varepsilon)$ fraction of optimal revenue? In particular: is $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ menu size enough for fixed $\varepsilon$, and what is the exact two-item exponent in $1/\varepsilon$?
open_problem: (i) for fixed $\varepsilon$, does $C(n,\varepsilon)$ grow polynomially in $n$, or is it exponential? (ii) determine the exact exponent $c$ with $C(2,\varepsilon)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-c})$.
background: Myerson's theory makes single-item revenue maximization simple: the optimal mechanism is a posted price (for one buyer) or a virtual-value auction. Multi-item revenue maximization is drastically different. By the taxation principle, any mechanism for a single buyer is equivalent to a menu of (lottery, price) options, and Hart and Nisan showed the revenue-optimal menu can be startlingly complex: even for two independent items, optimal mechanisms may need randomization, and for correlated items the optimal revenue may be infinite while every finite-menu mechanism earns only a negligible fraction — an infinite 'menu-size complexity'. This motivated menu size as a clean complexity measure for mechanisms, quantifying the 'simple versus optimal' tension at the heart of multidimensional mechanism design. Two regimes anchor the theory. First, constant-factor approximation is cheap: Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg showed the better of selling separately and grand bundling (a menu of $n+1$ options) achieves a constant fraction of optimal revenue for an additive buyer over independent items. Second, near-optimal approximation is subtle: Babaioff, Gonczarowski, and Nisan resolved the qualitative question by proving a finite menu of size $C(n,\varepsilon)$ always suffices for $(1-\varepsilon)$-optimal revenue, and Gonczarowski's optimal-transport-duality lower bound of $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ (two i.i.d. items from nice distributions) shows real growth is necessary. What is not known is the quantitative rate: whether $C(n,\varepsilon)$ can be polynomial in $n$ for fixed $\varepsilon$ (the known exponential lower bounds only kick in when $\varepsilon\approx 1/n$), and even the exact exponent of $1/\varepsilon$ for two items, where the bounds $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ leave a polynomial gap. These questions connect to communication complexity, mechanism descriptions in practice, and the buy-many literature.
full_statement: A monopolist sells $n$ items to a single additive, risk-neutral, quasilinear buyer whose item values are drawn from a product distribution $F=F_1\times\cdots\times F_n$. By the taxation principle a mechanism is a menu $\{(x_k,p_k)\}_k$ of lottery-price pairs, where $x_k\in[0,1]^n$ gives allocation probabilities and $p_k\in\mathbb{R}$ a price; the buyer picks a utility-maximizing entry. The menu size of a mechanism is its number of entries. Let $\mathrm{Rev}(F)$ be the optimal (unbounded-menu) revenue and define $$C(n,\varepsilon)=\min\{s:\ \forall F\ \exists\ \text{menu of size}\le s\ \text{with revenue}\ge(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{Rev}(F)\}.$$ Known: $C(n,\varepsilon)$ is finite for all $n,\varepsilon>0$ (Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan); exponential lower bounds are known in the regime $\varepsilon\sim 1/n$; for $n=2$, $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})\le C(2,\varepsilon)\le O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ (the upper bound under standard distributional assumptions; $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ unconditionally). Open: (i) for fixed $\varepsilon$, does $C(n,\varepsilon)$ grow polynomially in $n$, or is it exponential? (ii) determine the exact exponent $c$ with $C(2,\varepsilon)=\Theta(\varepsilon^{-c})$.
known_results: Foundational negatives: Hart, Nisan (EC 2013 / JET 2019) show optimal mechanisms for two independent items may require randomization, and for correlated items every finite menu can miss almost all revenue (infinite menu-size complexity), so finite-menu guarantees require independence. Constant factors are cheap: Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, Weinberg (FOCS 2014) show max(SRev, BRev) — a menu of $n+1$ entries — is a $6$-approximation (constant since improved). Near-optimality: Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan (STOC 2017 / GEB 2022) prove $C(n,\varepsilon)$ is finite for every $n,\varepsilon$, with upper bounds exponential in $n$, and exponential lower bounds when $\varepsilon\approx 1/n$. For two items, Hart-Nisan gave $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$; Gonczarowski (STOC 2018) strengthened this to $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ under standard economic assumptions and proved the first lower bound $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$, even for i.i.d. values from nice distributions; as a corollary the deterministic communication complexity of $(1-\varepsilon)$-optimal two-item mechanisms is $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. Related strands: buy-many mechanisms have $\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\varepsilon)$ menu-size complexity in some regimes (Chawla, Teng, Tzamos, EC 2020), symmetric menu complexity of i.i.d. items is quasi-polynomial (Kothari et al. 2019), and communication/quantum-communication analogues have been studied through ITCS 2025. As of mid-2026, both headline quantitative questions — polynomial-in-$n$ menu size for fixed $\varepsilon$, and the tight two-item exponent in $[1/4,2]$ — remain open.

progress.summary: No movement on the two core quantitative questions since Gonczarowski (STOC 2018): the two-item gap $[\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4}), O(\varepsilon^{-2})]$ and the poly-vs-exponential growth of $C(n,\varepsilon)$ in $n$ for fixed $\varepsilon$ both stand as of mid-2026. Activity has shifted to adjacent models: buy-many mechanisms (poly menu-size complexity in restricted settings), symmetric menus for i.i.d. items, and the communication and quantum-communication complexity of auctions (e.g. ITCS 2025), which refine but do not resolve the menu-size questions.

counterexample_rationale: Improved lower bounds are explicit constructions: one must exhibit a (family of) product distributions and prove every small menu loses more than an $\varepsilon$ fraction of revenue. Candidate distributions can be searched numerically (the optimal two-item mechanism is computable via convex programming for discretized instances), but converting numerical evidence into a proof requires duality certificates, so this is construction-friendly rather than purely finite-checkable.
alphaevolve_rationale: An evolutionary loop could search over two-item value distributions (e.g. parameterized densities or discrete grids), compute optimal revenue and best size-$s$ menu revenue via LP/convex optimization, and evolve instances maximizing the gap — directly attacking the $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$-vs-$O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ question with candidate worst cases; optimal-transport duality then offers a route to certify the discovered gaps.

literature.synthesis: The upper-bound technology is 'nudge and round': Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan (STOC 2017 / GEB 2022) discretize the menu of an optimal mechanism, rounding allocations and prices so the buyer's choice changes little and revenue loses only $\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{Rev}$, giving finiteness of $C(n,\varepsilon)$ but with bounds exponential in $n$; their lower bounds show exponential size is genuinely necessary when the accuracy target scales as $\varepsilon\sim 1/n$. Gonczarowski (STOC 2018) introduced the main lower-bound tool at fixed $n$: the optimal-transport (Daskalakis-Deckelbaum-Tzamos) duality characterizing optimal two-item mechanisms, from which he extracted the $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ bound and, in the positive direction, an $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ menu under standard assumptions, plus the tight $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ communication complexity for fixed $n$. Hart and Nisan's JET 2019 paper delimits the whole program: with correlated items no finite menu achieves any constant fraction of optimal revenue, so product distributions are essential. Adjacent lines: Babaioff-Immorlica-Lucier-Weinberg's constant-factor 'SRev vs BRev' result shows tiny menus suffice for constant approximation; Chawla, Teng, Tzamos show buy-many mechanisms — a natural robustness restriction — have polynomial menu-size complexity, suggesting the exponential blowup is tied to exotic one-shot lotteries; Kothari, Mohan, Schvartzman, Singla, Weinberg bound symmetric menu complexity for i.i.d. items at quasi-polynomial. The two-item exponent gap persists because the lower-bound construction exploits only local behavior of the transport dual near a critical region, while the upper bound rounds globally; closing it likely requires either a sharper duality-based construction or a fundamentally better rounding that adapts menu density to the distribution.

reviewed.ref: Hart, Nisan, 'Selling Multiple Correlated Goods: Revenue Maximization and Menu-Size Complexity', EC 2013 / Journal of Economic Theory 2019
reviewed.result: Introduces menu-size complexity; shows randomization is needed for two independent items and that with correlated items every finite menu can lose almost all revenue; $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ menu for two independent items.

reviewed.ref: Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, Weinberg, 'A Simple and Approximately Optimal Mechanism for an Additive Buyer', FOCS 2014 / JACM 2020
reviewed.result: max(sell separately, grand bundle) — menu size $n+1$ — achieves a constant fraction (originally $1/6$) of optimal revenue for an additive buyer over independent items.

reviewed.ref: Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan, 'The Menu-Size Complexity of Revenue Approximation', STOC 2017 / Games and Economic Behavior 2022
reviewed.result: $C(n,\varepsilon)$ is finite for all $n,\varepsilon$: a menu of bounded size extracts $(1-\varepsilon)$ of optimal revenue; complementary exponential lower bounds in the regime $\varepsilon\approx 1/n$.

reviewed.ref: Gonczarowski, 'Bounding the Menu-Size of Approximately Optimal Auctions via Optimal-Transport Duality', STOC 2018
reviewed.result: Two items: lower bound $\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1/4})$ (even i.i.d. nice distributions) and upper bound $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ under standard assumptions; deterministic communication complexity $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ for fixed $n$.

reviewed.ref: Chawla, Teng, Tzamos, 'Menu-size Complexity and Revenue Continuity of Buy-many Mechanisms', EC 2020
reviewed.result: For buy-many mechanisms (buyer may purchase any multiset of menu entries), polynomial menu size suffices for near-optimal buy-many revenue, contrasting with the exponential blowup for unrestricted mechanisms.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: For the two-item lower bound: use the optimal-transport duality to construct distributions whose optimal menus have many 'essentially distinct' entries — a parameterized search over densities with numerical solution of the two-item screening problem (an infinite-dimensional LP, tractable after discretization) could locate candidates, then duality certificates make the bound rigorous. For upper bounds: adaptive rounding of menus (finer near high-curvature regions of the utility function) could plausibly beat $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$; for the $n$-item question, either extend nudge-and-round with dimension-free discretization (suggesting poly(n)) or lift the $\varepsilon\sim 1/n$ exponential lower bound to constant $\varepsilon$ via direct-sum-style constructions.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A lower-bound claim must exhibit distributions and prove EVERY menu of size $s$ loses $>\varepsilon\cdot\mathrm{Rev}$ — referees should check the argument covers randomized (lottery) entries, not just deterministic bundle prices, and that optimal revenue is certified from below (e.g. an explicit mechanism) while small-menu revenue is bounded from above (duality). An upper-bound claim must construct, for an arbitrary product distribution in the stated class, a small menu with certified revenue; check the distributional assumptions (bounded support? MHR?) match the claim's generality. Discretized instances are machine-checkable via LP, but the headline bounds are asymptotic statements requiring proof.

where_posed.text: Menu size as a complexity measure and the approximation question were introduced in Hart, Nisan, 'The Menu-Size Complexity of Auctions', EC 2013 (published as 'Selling Multiple Correlated Goods: Revenue Maximization and Menu-Size Complexity', Journal of Economic Theory 2019); the quantitative open questions are stated in Babaioff, Gonczarowski, Nisan, 'The Menu-Size Complexity of Revenue Approximation', STOC 2017 / Games and Economic Behavior 2022, and Gonczarowski, STOC 2018.
